items.title: ‘Completely Unscorched!’: Kathy Ireland Praises God After Husband’s Miracle Survival, Reveals Bible Survived Fire
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Former supermodel and businesswoman Kathy Ireland is praising God for her husband Greg’s survival after the engine of his commercial […]
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Former supermodel and businesswoman Kathy Ireland is praising God for her husband Greg’s survival after the engine of his commercial fishing boat caught fire and he miraculously survived.

Ireland revealed on Instagram that the boat was entirely destroyed, with one item notably surviving the harrowing ordeal: a Bible.

“Greg went to the harbor to assess the damage,” she wrote. “The boat and all its contents are no more. Besides our commercial fishing licenses, the only thing on the boat that survived is his Bible! Completely unscorched! My heart is overflowing full!”

Ireland shared remarkable images of the torched vessel and the totally pristine Bible, sparking awe from friends and fans.

In an earlier post, she initially described the difficult nature of losing the fishing boat.

“Life is really hard and really beautiful,” Ireland wrote in an Instagram description of a video showing the boat on fire. “God is great. I’m on the road for business and grandchildren so Greg was out alone. Engine exploded and a fire quickly melted all navigation equipment and survival raft!”

The Kathy Ireland Worldwide founder went on to thank those who prayed and helped rescue Greg. Beyond all else, though, Ireland praised the Lord even amid so much loss.

“Most of all, we thank our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ for this miracle of his survival,” she said.

Ireland concluded her message with the text of Isaiah‬ ‭43‬:‭2‬, which reads, “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; And through the rivers, they will not overflow you. When you walk through the fire, you will not be scorched, Nor will the flame burn you.”

Continue praying for Ireland and her family as they cope with the fallout of this tragedy.

items.title: Senator Intensely Questions Cissie Graham Lynch on LGBT Views During Confirmation Hearing
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: Important.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine (D) intensely questioned Cissie Graham Lynch, the granddaughter of the late Rev. Billy Graham, on LGBT issues during her Senate confirmation hearing to serve as ambassador-at-large for international religious freedom.

Listen to the latest episode of the “Quick Start” podcast

Kaine asked Lynch, who supports a biblical understanding of marriage as a lifelong union between one male and one female, how she would work as ambassador “to protect … LGBTQ folks from persecution.” Lynch immediately responded that, in her official capacity, she would have a “responsibility to protect people of all faiths” and does not believe “anyone should ever be criminalized or persecuted for their personal beliefs.”

The senator, who identifies as Catholic, told Lynch there are “countries around the world [that] criminalize just being gay, being LGBTQ” — an interesting line of inquiry for a politician who has been intensely supportive of celebrating Islam, stating in the past that Muslim Americans “enrich the fabric of our communities,” given the religion is deeply opposed to homosexuality.

Kaine pressed Lynch to explain her view, which she expressed in February 2021, that certain LGBT nondiscrimination laws could jeopardize Christian religious freedoms, a concept that apparently was difficult for the Virginia lawmaker to understand. For context, Lynch — who has worked alongside her father, Franklin Graham, at the humanitarian organization Samaritan’s Purse — wrote in a 2021 opinion article for Fox News that the “extreme” Equality Act would “erode” religious liberties for Christians.

If enacted into law, the Equality Act, which has been introduced in Congress numerous times but has never passed through the Senate, would amend existing civil rights laws in the U.S. to explicitly prohibit any form of discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity across areas like employment, housing, and education. Lynch, for her part, has argued such legislation would override religious liberty protections, barring faith-based organizations that hold to a biblical view of sexuality from operating according to their deeply held religious convictions.

During her Senate hearing this week, Lynch specifically mentioned to Kaine the case of baker Jack Phillips, a small business owner in Denver, Colorado, who skyrocketed to national news in 2012, when he declined to make a custom wedding cake for a same-sex couple. He has faced numerous lawsuits in the years since for similar issues, all of which he has won to date.

Nevertheless, Lynch argued Phillips is a prime example of an American who has faced intense attacks because of his personally held religious beliefs when it comes to marriage. She also mentioned he has never turned away customers due to their sexual practices or personal ideologies, noting Phillips “for years” has “served people of the LGBT community” without issue.

Listen to the latest episode of the “Radical Revelations” podcast

While the ambassador-at-large nominee has her own views of sexuality and marriage, she told the senators in Congress she has always sought to engage in dialogue about these issues “with kindness” and “with respect.”

“I’ve talked about on my platform many issues that are divisive in our culture and we are in a culture that teaches us that, if we believe something differently, that we can’t get along with somebody, that that’s hate speech,” she said.

On a global scale, Lynch said she “would never be able to support something [such as a Ugandan law] where it’s criminalizing people … for their sexual identity, for their sexual preference.” She reaffirmed to Kaine she is committed, if confirmed, to “represent[ing] people of all faiths,” and drew particular attention to the religious persecution happening around the world: “People are dying. People are being persecuted. People are put into jail. There’s 80 countries with blasphemy laws.”

“I’ve learned that through my years of working when I work in the countries with people I often don’t have the same beliefs, but we come together,” she said of her humanitarian work with Samaritan’s Purse, adding her goal is to “find that common ground to help people on a bipartisan mission.”

Before a vote on Lynch’s confirmation can reach the full Senate, she must first be approved by the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, where Republicans currently hold a 12-10 majority. In the full Senate, Republicans outnumber Democrats at 53-47.

items.title: Anthony Ippolito Bet on Himself to Play Young Sylvester Stallone. It’s One of the Best Performances of the Year.
items.author: Cameron Strang
items.summary: By the time anyone in Hollywood wanted Sylvester Stallone’s boxing script, he and his wife, Sasha, were down to their last $106. Producers Robert Chartoff and Irwin Winkler saw it as a star vehicle for someone like Burt Reynolds or Robert Redford, and they offered the unknown writer $75,000 fo
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

By the time anyone in Hollywood wanted Sylvester Stallone’s boxing script, he and his wife, Sasha, were down to their last $106. Producers Robert Chartoff and Irwin Winkler saw it as a star vehicle for someone like Burt Reynolds or Robert Redford, and they offered the unknown writer $75,000 for it, according to TCM. When he refused, the offer went to $100,000, then $150,000. Stallone’s condition never moved. He would sell Rocky only if he got to play Rocky.

Nearly 50 years later, Anthony Ippolito made his own version of that bet. “No one asked me to audition for this,” he told RELEVANT. “I just heard the project was getting made and really wanted to get into the conversation.” He sees some of himself in Stallone’s story, and he expects other people will too. “Hopefully a lot of people in creative fields feel that way once they see the film and see what he went through.”

It paid off. In I Play Rocky, Peter Farrelly’s film about how Rocky got made, Ippolito gives a stunning performance as a young Stallone, broke and stubborn and still years from fame, and the movie around him is every bit as good. It opened in select theaters Nov. 6 and expands nationwide Nov. 20.

“It’s very tempting in a position like that to go in the other direction and just say thanks for the money,” Ippolito says of Stallone’s choice. “But it’s not what he decided to do. We wouldn’t be sitting here talking about him fifty years later if he went the other way with it.” He calls the money Stallone turned down “a remarkable amount” and the choice “very, very tough.”

The film covers roughly 1972 to 1976: the broke New York years, the drive west, the script Stallone wrote after watching underdog Chuck Wepner go 15 rounds with Muhammad Ali, the standoff over who would star in it and a shoot that nearly came apart. It ends before the world knew who Sylvester Stallone was.

“He’s known for what he became, as a big star,” Ippolito says. “This movie’s about something entirely different. Just stripping all that away and focusing on what he was like before that.”

To prepare, Ippolito spent a long stretch hunting down footage of Stallone from the early ’70s. “It was tough because he wasn’t a big name at this time,” he says. “But I tried to find whatever I could.”

He also talked with Stallone over Zoom. “It’s incredibly informative, what he was willing to share with me, and I just appreciated his vulnerability,” Ippolito says. “I know it’s not easy to talk about some of this stuff in one’s life. He was in a pretty dark period of time before Rocky got made. So just telling me some of the little details about what that period of time was like was huge.”

Watch our conversation with Ippolito on The RELEVANT Podcast:

In the film, Stallone is living close to the edge, working low-paying jobs between auditions, with a father, played by Matt Dillon, who doesn’t think much of his son’s ambitions. AnnaSophia Robb plays Sasha, who pushes him to use his real name and to start writing. Later, the film follows the shoot itself: a punishing schedule, a director, John G. Avildsen (Jay Duplass), who wants most scenes done in a single take, and producers scrambling to cover a budget shortfall.

Then there was the boxing, which Ippolito had never done. “I had to figure out how to do that,” he says. “It was tricky, but we figured it out.” The work came in small pieces: learning to hit a speed bag, going over fight choreography with Stephan James, who plays Carl Weathers, and building the rest “piece by piece.” Between the fights and the famous training montage, Ippolito says the montage was harder. “We were doing a lot of that stuff in December in Philly, and it was pretty cold,” he says. “The whole crew was kind of battling the elements. Neither was a walk in the park.”

Critics have mostly come away impressed. On Rotten Tomatoes, the film holds an 86 percent score, and the site’s critics consensus singles out Ippolito’s “uncanny embodiment” of Stallone. Variety’s Owen Gleiberman wrote that the film understands how the underdog story on screen echoed the one it took to get Rocky made in the first place.

United Artists finally agreed to let Stallone star, but on a budget of about $1 million, and only after Chartoff and Winkler put up a completion bond to cover any overruns, according to TCM. Stallone took the standard writer’s fee and $20,000 to play the part. “As far as I was concerned, if I didn’t get this part it was the only shot I would ever get,” Stallone said later. “I was willing to do it for nothing.”

“When people saw the original Rocky, they walked out feeling empowered and hopeful, and hopefully they had a fun time in the theater,” Ippolito says. “It’s pretty similar with this one. That’s the goal.”

Rocky won Best Picture. The writer who wouldn’t sell it without himself attached was nominated for best actor and best original screenplay.

items.title: What the Son Kept: Microchimerism and the Incarnation
items.author: H. S. Theophilus
items.summary:
H. S. Theophilus

Mother and child do more than share a womb; they give something of themselves to each other.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

H. S. Theophilus

A mother never stops carrying her child.

We have always understood this as a figure of speech. The bond between mother and child endures long after the cord is cut.

In 1996, researchers discovered that the saying was truer than we knew. They found genetic evidence of male cells in the blood of women who had given birth to sons. In one woman, that evidence was still detectable twenty-seven years after the birth of her last son. Such cells can cross the placenta during pregnancy and remain long afterward. Later studies have found evidence of them in mothers’ livers, thyroids, hearts, and even brains.

The phenomenon is called microchimerism, a name borrowed from the Chimera of Greek mythology, a monster part lion, part goat, and part serpent. An unlikely name for something that speaks so tenderly of the union between a mother and her child.

It seems, then, that a mother may carry her child not only in her memory but in her flesh.

For a Christian, that discovery is hard to contemplate without thinking of another mother: a young woman of Nazareth who carried the eternal Word made flesh within her womb.

And what did her Son keep of her?

Catholics were quick to see what this discovery might mean for Mary, and over the past several years, a number of articles and homilies have explored it. Their reasoning is beautiful in its simplicity: If mothers keep their children’s cells, then Mary may well have carried cells of Jesus until the end of her earthly life. In this light, Mary’s assumption into heaven takes on a new and moving significance: The body that sheltered something of Christ was not left to the grave.

These reflections have done something valuable. They help many Catholics see the incarnation with fresh wonder, revealing how discoveries about the natural world can deepen our appreciation of the mysteries of faith.

Yet they rest on a possibility rather than a certainty. We cannot know whether Mary retained cells from Jesus.

Here theology sheds its own light. Divinity cannot be passed along through cells. In Christ, the divine and human natures are united in the one person of the Word, and nothing Mary may have retained would make her body divine. The assumption is above all a gift of grace, one that the wonders of biology can help us contemplate. Mary is the Mother of God because of who her Son is, not because of what may have remained in her bloodstream.

But there is another side to this remarkable discovery. What if we followed the cells in the other direction? Microchimerism is not a one-way street. Just as the child’s cells enter the mother, the mother’s cells enter the child. In 1999, researchers found that maternal cells could persist in adults, some in their forties. Some of us, it seems, still carry something of our mother’s body.

The physician Kristin Collier, writing in Church Life Journal, called this “radical mutuality at the cellular level.” Mother and child do more than share a womb; they give something of themselves to each other.

In the case of Jesus, however, there is a far greater truth that needs no laboratory to establish. Conceived by the Holy Spirit without a human father, Christ received his human nature from his mother. What he took from her was not a trace but his very flesh: the face the disciples knew, the hands that would be pierced, the body that suffered on the Cross and rose from the tomb. It was no borrowed or merely apparent body. God sent his Son, St. Paul writes, “born of a woman.” Every Sunday, the Church confesses that he “was incarnate of the Virgin Mary, and became man.”

A medieval treatise on the assumption by the author known as Pseudo-Augustine gathered the whole mystery into a single phrase: caro Jesu caro est Mariae, “the flesh of Jesus is the flesh of Mary.”

Seen this way, the wonder only deepens. It is a marvel that Mary may have carried cells of her Son. It is a greater marvel still that God kept the flesh he received from Mary.

Before Mary was ever assumed body and soul into heaven, the flesh she gave Jesus had passed through death and resurrection and was already glorified at the right hand of the Father. Her assumption, then, takes on a particular beauty: The mother is graciously drawn by her Son into the glory he had entered before her.

The Church’s tradition has long contemplated this bond. St. John Damascene, whom Pope Pius XII cites in Munificentissimus Deus, saw how fitting it was that she who had carried the Creator as a child at her breast should dwell in the divine tabernacles. For John Damascene, Mary’s assumption rests not on any biological necessity but on her unique relationship with her Son. And that relationship began with the gift of her flesh to him.

Between Mary and her Son, the giving runs both ways. The Church has an ancient name for the greater mystery at work here: the wondrous exchange. On January 1, the Solemnity of Mary, Mother of God, the Church sings of it in an antiphon that has been prayed since the Middle Ages, “O admirabile commercium,” “O wondrous exchange! The Creator of the human race, taking a living body, was pleased to be born of a virgin; and coming forth as man without human seed, He has bestowed on us His divinity.”

In this exchange, God takes what is ours and gives us what is his. As St. Irenaeus put it, the Word became what we are so that he might bring us to be what he is. And the exchange takes place in Mary. The Second Vatican Council says she received the Word “in her heart and in her body.” In her womb, our nature was handed to God, and through her Son, his life is handed back to us.

Here, microchimerism offers Christian reflection one of its most beautiful gifts. St. John Paul II described faith and reason as two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth. In this case, science gives faith an image written into the body itself. During pregnancy, mother and child exchange living cells, some of which may persist long after birth. It is a small, created echo of the wondrous exchange.

In Mary’s womb, the wondrous exchange entered human history, a mystery that would reach its saving fulfillment through the cross and resurrection.

But the exchange that began in Mary does not end with her. What God accomplished in her, he means to accomplish in all his people. That is why the Second Vatican Council calls her, glorified in body and soul, “the image and beginning of the Church as it is to be perfected in the world to come” and “a sign of sure hope.” She received Christ in her body; we receive him through the sacraments.

In Holy Communion, we receive the flesh Christ took from Mary, now risen and glorified. The Church sings it plainly in the Eucharistic hymn “Ave verum corpus, natum de Maria Virgine,” “Hail, true body, born of the Virgin Mary.” Here, the comparison with microchimerism reaches its limit. In microchimerism, cells from one person may persist within the body of another. The Eucharist is a mystery of an entirely different order: We receive Christ himself, body, blood, soul, and divinity, truly present under the sacramental signs, and through that communion, we are drawn more deeply into his life. St. Augustine heard Christ say to him, “You will not change me into yourself like bodily food; but you will be changed into me.”

We do not take in a trace of Christ. We are taken up into him.

And Mary shows us where this exchange is leading. “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life,” Jesus promised, “and I will raise him on the last day.” Her assumption, the Catechism teaches, is an anticipation of the resurrection of other Christians. What happened to her is a foretaste of what is promised to us.

What a curious irony that a phenomenon named after a monster should reveal something so profound about being human.

We live in an age that tells us we belong only to ourselves, and our bodies are ours to manage or remake as we choose. Microchimerism tells a quieter story. Human life begins not in isolation, but in dependence upon another. Even before birth, our bodies bear witness to bonds we were given before we could choose them, beginning with our mothers. The human body is not merely biological material, but a gift received.

The Christian faith goes further still. God did not save the world from a distance. He took flesh from a human mother, and through that flesh he gives his own life to all of us.

In the icon of Our Lady of Perpetual Help, the Christ Child, confronted with the instruments of his passion, clings to his mother’s hand. His own small hands took shape within her womb.

We marvel that a mother may carry her child for the rest of her life. The greater wonder is that the Child chose to carry his mother.

items.title: Hate Your Neighbor as Yourself?
items.author: Dr. Richard Clements
items.summary:
Dr. Richard Clements

If you don’t love yourself in a healthy way, then you will find it difficult, perhaps impossible, to truly love other people.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Richard Clements

Sadly, tragically, there seems to be a lot of hatred in the world today. Where is all of this hate coming from? Several causes come to mind:

  • The internet and social media have contributed significantly to the amplification and rapid spread of hatred. Activists, podcasters, influencers, and others who express strong emotions such as hatred tend to get more clicks, and their passionate and hate-filled posts are more likely to get shared and go viral than more rational, civil, and nuanced expressions of political and cultural opinion. The extensive indulgence in hatred on social media also makes hate seem more common and widespread than it is in the general population.
  • In our increasingly secular age, many people have made politics their new religion, ascribing ultimate rather than relative importance to politics and political issues. When politics becomes the central focus of a person’s life, civil and reasonable discussion regarding political issues can easily get supplanted by a bitter and vitriolic hatred for anyone who dares to voice even the slightest disagreement with one’s own opinions.
  • Cynical politicians often foment and encourage such hatred, knowing that stirring up strong emotions like anger and hatred can generate political activism and support for their candidacies and their policies.
  • We fallen human beings are prone to envy and resentment of those who seem to have a better life than we do, and we sometimes look to scapegoat other individuals or groups as being the cause of our problems and disappointments.

Undoubtedly, all of these factors (and others) have contributed to the rising levels of hatred in contemporary society. But one of the deepest causes of the increasing hatred of other people is the increasing hatred of oneself.

St. Augustine wisely observed, “If you do not know how to love yourself, you cannot truthfully love your neighbor.” The ability to genuinely love other people is crucially dependent on the ability to love oneself. If you don’t love yourself in a healthy way, then you will find it difficult, perhaps impossible, to truly love other people.

That’s why Jesus assumed love of self in expressing the second greatest commandment (“You shall love your neighbor as yourself”—Matt 22:36-40; Mark 12:28-34; Luke 10:25-37), and that’s also why this inextricable connection between the ability to love oneself and the ability to love other people is emphasized over and over again in Scripture (Lev 19:18; Matt 5:43, 19:19; Rom 13:9; Gal 5:14; Jas 2:8). Jesus, and Scripture as a whole, establish self-love as the standard for all love among human beings.

Surely there is no lack of self-love in the world today, when we live in an era of rampant egocentrism and even narcissism? But of course, egocentrism and narcissism are not genuine or healthy forms of self-love. Egoism and narcissism are often attempts to compensate for an actual lack of self-love. For many, there is an emptiness inside of them, a void that they’re trying to fill up through an exaggerated sense of self-importance, the gratification of their excessively self-centered desires, and efforts to convince others of their greatness or uniqueness.

But it’s not just egoists and narcissists who suffer from a lack of healthy self-love. There are many other people today who, although they may not be egoists or narcissists, also fail to develop or maintain a healthy love of self. All of these people, whether egoists or not, tend to lack two of the key elements of love: approval of the beloved (in this case, oneself) as good, and willing the good of the beloved.

In order to be able to love anyone genuinely, you need to be able to see good of some sort in that person, as Josef Pieper pointed out:

In every conceivable case love signifies much the same as approval. This is first of all to be taken in the literal sense of the word’s root: loving someone or something means finding him or it probus, the Latin word for “good.” It is a way of turning to him or it and saying, “It’s good that you exist; it’s good that you are in this world!” 

In order to be able to love ourselves in a healthy way, we need to be able to approve of ourselves, to see some good in ourselves, to be able to say to ourselves, “It’s good that you exist!” Many people today find that difficult to believe about themselves.

It’s also difficult for many people to will their own good today—or better said, to will their true good rather than what they mistake for their good. Many people today are confused about where their good truly lies, and they end up seeking fulfillment via goods that will never truly fill them up (money, status, fame, power, etc.) instead of more fulfilling goods (loving relationships with other people, meaningful work, and a sense of purpose in life) and the ultimate good, God.

So the question of why so many people today find it difficult to love themselves in a healthy way is, in part, a question of why so many people find it difficult to see the good in themselves and to know where their true good lies. Why is that?
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

Once again, there are certainly multiple potential causes here, but two of the main causes for the lack of healthy self-love today are also the causes of many of our other societal problems: the prevalence of broken families and the loss—or outright rejection—of faith in God.

Parents are typically our first exposure to love. We need and want our parents to see the good in us and to will our genuine good. With the increase in broken families, fewer of us experience such approval and loving care. It’s difficult for us to love ourselves when the people who should love us the most and the people we most need to love us when we are young don’t seem to truly love us.

Also, as Hans Urs von Balthasar has emphasized, our parents are not only the source of our first exposure to love; they are also our first exposure to the beauty, goodness, and truth of the world and of life itself and, most importantly, our first exposure to the God who is love.

Which brings us to the other fundamental cause of a lack of healthy self-love: the rejection of God in our increasingly secular society. Our ultimate good as human beings is ut in Deo sit—that we might be in God. Our ultimate good is that we might share in the divine life and love (2 Pet 1:4). We crave God’s love, whether or not some of us will admit that craving to ourselves. Even Jean-Paul Sartre, an inveterate atheist, is quoted as having acknowledged, “That God does not exist, I cannot deny; that my whole being cries out for God I cannot forget.”

The deepest source of genuine self-love is knowing that we are loved by God, as Balthasar has also explained:

I only appreciate fully that God is my “highest good” when I learn (in the Son) that I am a “good” to him, affirmed by him; this is what guarantees my being and my freedom. And it is only when I learn that I represent a “good” and a “thou” to God that I can fully trust in the imparted gift of being and freedom and so, affirmed from and by eternity, really affirm myself too.

When you hate yourself, it’s easy to hate other people. But when you can see yourself as good and lovable in God’s eyes, it’s easier to love yourself, and then it becomes easier to love other people too.
